kaigo-atomic-nonverbal-dialogue.heading: Adapt listening posture, distance and touch
paragraphs: Expressions and actions are important clues for understanding someone, but the same gesture may have several meanings. Do not decide feelings from expression alone; check together with their words and the situation.

Facing the person at eye level instead of looking down can reduce pressure. Check a comfortable degree of eye contact. Not looking into your eyes does not prove they are not listening, and do not require sustained eye contact to show understanding.

A slow, calm voice and pauses for replies help the person receive information and answer. Staff nods and brief responses can show listening. However, one nod by the person does not establish understanding of an explanation or consent to specific help. Check the necessary content separately.

Crossed arms or legs or a body leaning away can seem unapproachable in some situations, but meanings vary with culture, individual and physical conditions. Do not judge personality from one posture. Face the person comfortably and check responses.

Some find closeness or hand-holding reassuring, others uncomfortable. Cultural knowledge cannot replace asking the person’s wishes. Timing, force and frequency also affect touch. Explain its purpose, check an acceptable method and stop that contact if refused.

[Learning example] The person steps back when a worker approaches. Rather than approaching again because “everyone here is friendly,” maintain a comfortable distance and ask where to stand for conversation. Even necessary care contact requires explanation and checking of purpose and method.
This section teaches meanings and reasons for checking. Actual support follows condition, wishes, individual care plans and facility instruction. Do not independently start an unclear method.

kaigo-atomic-shared-care-records.heading: Pass condition, assistance and responses to the next worker
paragraphs: Sharing information with healthcare professionals as well as care workers supports the person’s life as a team. Records aim to improve support quality and maintain necessary checks and help across staff changes, rather than merely fill forms.

Plans describe future help, case records document progress, and handoffs pass necessary information to the next worker. Meetings and direct conversations also support consultation, but speaking alone does not establish that every necessary record remains. Distinguish plans from implementation.

Record according to facility procedures on the same day and as promptly as possible, identifying when events happened. Do not confuse event and writing times when they differ. Separately record condition, actual help and subsequent responses.

Separate the source of “It hurts” from staff-observed skin changes or measurements. When conveying medical assessment, identify whose judgment it is rather than implying diagnosis from care-worker observation. Do not invent unconfirmed values or responses to make records look complete.

The receiver also notes key points, repeats what was heard and asks questions. Sharing what is handed over and who checks next helps identify omissions and misunderstandings. Handle information with appropriate recipients and in suitable locations; do not spread private details to unrelated people.

[Learning example] A handoff saying only “Everything is fine” does not tell the receiver what was done or which responses were checked. Confirm and add times, condition, assistance, actual responses and unknowns, then agree on next observations and roles.
This section teaches meanings and reasons for checking. Actual support follows condition, wishes, individual care plans and facility instruction. Do not independently start an unclear method.

kaigo-atomic-movement-body-labels.heading: Describe body location and sides specifically
paragraphs: Muscles, bones and joints contribute to movement. Distinguish head, neck, chest, abdomen, back, lower back and buttocks when describing location. Instead of summarizing everything as bodily discomfort, check where the person points to inform reporting.

For upper limbs, distinguish shoulder, arm, elbow, wrist, palm and back of the hand. Define sides from the person’s body, not reversed from the facing worker’s viewpoint. Confirm the indicated palm or opposite back surface with the person before reporting.

For lower limbs, distinguish leg, knee, ankle, heel and sole. The sole means the underside, not only the heel. Separate the indicated location and the person’s account of onset and sensation from what staff actually observed.

Knowing a body-area name differs from knowing a diagnosis or suitable transfer method. Check pain, available movement, abilities and plan and tell the necessary person. Do not independently pull limbs to investigate disease while locating a complaint.

[Learning example] Saying “My hand hurts,” the person points to the back of the right hand. Ask whether that is the correct location and record the site, time and words. Observe appearance separately and do not invent the pain’s cause.
This section teaches meanings and reasons for checking. Actual support follows condition, wishes, individual care plans and facility instruction. Do not independently start an unclear method.

kaigo-atomic-visual-guided-walking.heading: Share pace and route changes before moving
paragraphs: Before guiding someone with reduced vision, introduce yourself and ask whether and how they want help. Match their pace rather than pulling at staff speed. Check equipment, abilities and route before moving.

Describe corners, steps and floor changes before reaching them. Using an agreed reference such as directions from the person’s viewpoint helps them anticipate and adjust. Explaining only after turning is too late for preparation.

The material’s guiding posture is one example of confirming wishes and sharing support. Do not assume identical touch is wanted by everyone. Follow preferences, facility-trained methods and responses during movement. Do not suddenly seize an arm or pull without checking wishes.

[Learning example] A worker pulls the person around a corner before explaining. Next time, describe direction and change beforehand, check pace and guiding method, then proceed. If route or assistance conditions are unsuitable, do not continue unchanged; check alternatives or needed help.
This section teaches meanings and reasons for checking. Actual support follows condition, wishes, individual care plans and facility instruction. Do not independently start an unclear method.

kaigo-language-session-1-notes.heading: Read suggestions, responsibilities and sequences
paragraphs: In learning conversation 209, the window seat is the worker’s suggestion, while the person wants a seat near the entrance. They still plan to attend the afternoon gathering and not go into the garden. Do not record the suggestion as the final choice or turn a seating preference into cancellation of the entire activity.

“I wrote it” means the speaker wrote it. “I had a senior colleague check it” includes a different person’s action. Distinguish who entered the number, checked the results and will sign the inspection sheet. Completed entry and checking do not necessarily mean a completed signature.

In the reservation-change conversation, “ask reception first” and “tell you after learning a change is possible” are important conditions. Wanting an earlier visit, confirmed change availability and actual departure are separate states. Telling a colleague the plan does not mean the change or departure is complete.

“First, next, afterward” describe the current task’s order. In conversation 212, check the date, show the person responsible and then post the notice. If an initial repeat-back is wrong, reread including the correction. Do not apply this notice sequence to transfers or other assistance.

Preserve the degree expressed in negatives such as “not bad.” Do not strengthen this to “very good” or expand it to no problems at all. Ask the person if concerns or severity need clarification. “Not very” or “not often” indicates limited degree or frequency; do not turn “does not speak much” into “does not speak at all.”

kaigo-reading-new-209.heading: Learning conversation: seating preference and participation
paragraphs:
Person: I will attend the afternoon gathering, but I will not go into the garden.
Worker: Shall I arrange a seat by the window?
Person: It is too bright there. I would prefer a seat near the entrance.
Worker: Near the entrance. I will check the room now.
Person: Please do. I have not canceled my participation.
Worker: Right. Only your seating preference has changed.

Reading: Participation in the afternoon gathering is not canceled. The person will not enter the garden and prefers the entrance rather than the suggested window seat. The worker will check the room, so a seat is not established as already arranged.

kaigo-reading-new-210.heading: Learning conversation: entry, checking and signature responsibilities
paragraphs:
Worker A: Is the wheelchair inspection sheet ready?
Worker B: I wrote the number. A senior colleague checked the results for me.
Worker A: So everything is finished?
Worker B: No, the signature is still missing.
Worker A: Who will sign?
Worker B: I will ask the senior colleague who checked it.

Reading: Worker B entered the number, and the senior colleague checked the results. The signature is outstanding, with a request planned for that colleague. Keep actions and responsibilities separate. Having someone check is neither checking it yourself nor a completed signature. This learning conversation does not prescribe actual wheelchair inspection methods.

kaigo-reading-new-211.heading: Learning conversation: do not confirm a change before checking
paragraphs:
Person: I would like to go to the library earlier.
Worker: First I will ask reception whether the reservation can be changed.
Person: Are we leaving right now?
Worker: No. I will let you know after confirming that a change is possible.
Person: All right. I will wait for a reply.
Worker: I will also tell another worker about the plan.

Reading: The worker will first ask reception whether the reservation can change, then inform the person after confirming availability. The person is waiting. Neither the time change nor departure is established as completed. Sharing a plan with a colleague is not completed implementation.

kaigo-reading-new-212.heading: Learning conversation: read the corrected sequence
paragraphs:
Worker A: Please prepare the notice. First check the date, next show it to the person responsible, and afterward post it.
Worker B: Post it and then show the person responsible?
Worker A: Those two are reversed.
Worker B: Check the date, have the person responsible check, then post it?
Worker A: Yes, that order for this notice, please.
Worker B: I will post it last.

Reading: The final order is date check, presentation to the person responsible, then posting. Worker B first reversed the last two but corrected the order. This sequence applies only to this notice request, not another task or care movement.

kaigo-language-session-1-terms.heading: Vocabulary for roles and plans
paragraphs: 希望（きぼう） — Wishes: what the person would like to do or have happen.
提案（ていあん） — Suggestion: offering an idea to someone, distinguished from the result they choose.
確認（かくにん） — Checking: asking or investigating uncertainty to establish reliable information.
参加（さんか） — Participation: joining a gathering or similar activity, checked separately from seating or location preferences.
点検表（てんけんひょう） — Inspection sheet: a form recording equipment checks or results; its presence alone does not establish completed inspection.
署名（しょめい） — Signature: writing one’s name, an action distinct from entering a number or checking results.
予約（よやく） — Reservation: arranging use in advance; check separately whether a change is possible or complete.
受付（うけつけ） — Reception: the desk or worker handling requests and inquiries; here, the recipient of a question about possible changes.
掲示（けいじ） — Posting: displaying information where people can see it; in this conversation it is planned after checks.
順序（じゅんじょ） — Sequence: the order of earlier and later actions, checked including any corrections.

kaigo-language-session-2-notes.heading: Read request scope, intake and display conditions
paragraphs: Check “sageru” through its object and context. Clearing dishes means removing used tableware, while lowering pants moves clothing down. “Samasu” means cooling; “atatameru” means warming. Reading a word does not establish a suitable personal temperature or cooking method.

Swallowing means the swallowing function; aspiration means food or liquid entering the airway below the vocal cords. Do not equate all swallowing difficulty with aspiration. Coughing or choking words describe responses or complaints, not diagnoses of cause or aspiration. They do not authorize independent thickening changes.

A menu is a combination of dishes, and a menu chart displays it. Record staple, side-dish and soup intake separately. “All staple, half the side dishes” does not establish unconfirmed soup intake. Grilled fish, deep-fried food and stir-fried dishes name cooking methods; the names do not establish prescribed personal amounts.

[Explain in your own words] Distinguish “thickness” from “thickening powder”: the former is liquid viscosity, the latter material used to adjust it. Next write a record with unknown soup intake. Example: “All staple, half the side dishes. Soup amount is unconfirmed; I plan to correct the record after checking.”

kaigo-reading-new-215.heading: Learning conversation: independent opening and reading help
paragraphs:
Person: I want to open the snack bag myself.
Worker: I will put it here, then.
Person: The name label is too small to read. Please read just that part.
Worker: I will read the label and hand you the unopened bag.
Person: Yes. I want to know what the snack is before eating.
Worker: Understood.

Reading: The person wants to open the bag themselves; the only requested help is reading the small name label. The worker plans to hand it over unopened. Difficulty seeing text does not establish inability to eat, chew or swallow.

kaigo-reading-new-216.heading: Learning conversation: separate staple, side-dish and soup amounts
paragraphs:
Worker A: I am checking lunch records. Were both staple and side dishes half eaten?
Worker B: All the staple and half the side dishes.
Worker A: What about soup?
Worker B: I have not checked yet.
Worker A: Then please do not write that everything was eaten.
Worker B: I will check the soup amount before correcting the record.

Reading: All the staple and half the side dishes were eaten, but soup amount is unconfirmed. Worker B plans to correct the record after checking soup. Neither complete intake of every item nor completed correction is stated.

kaigo-reading-new-217.heading: Learning conversation: preserve weekday conditions and undecided choices
paragraphs:
Person: Can I choose snack time next week too?
Worker: You can choose the time only on Wednesday.
Person: Can I choose a dining-room seat only that day too?
Worker: We ask seating preferences every day.
Person: Then Wednesday’s snack at three, please. I want to decide the seat that day.
Worker: Three for the time; the seat is still undecided.

Reading: At this fictional facility, snack time is selectable only on Wednesday, while seating preferences are asked daily. The person chose three o’clock for Wednesday’s snack. The seat remains undecided until the day. Do not merge the weekday condition with the daily seating check.

kaigo-reading-new-218.heading: Learning conversation: paper and large print together
paragraphs:
Person: I would like a menu. Is there a printed paper version in large text?
Worker: A tablet can enlarge the text.
Person: I would prefer paper, rather than a screen.
Worker: Small text on paper would be hard to read?
Person: Yes, I need both conditions.
Worker: I will check for a large-print paper version.

Reading: The person needs a printed paper menu with large text. Large screen text does not meet the paper condition, and small text on paper does not meet readability needs. The worker plans to check availability; it is not established as secured or delivered.

kaigo-language-session-2-terms.heading: Vocabulary reference when needed
paragraphs: 温める（あたためる） — To warm something by raising its temperature.
エプロン（えぷろん） — Apron: worn to protect clothing or similar surfaces from soiling.
嚥下（えんげ） — Swallowing: moving material from the mouth through the throat toward the esophagus.
きざむ（きざむ） — To chop food or other material finely.
誤嚥（ごえん） — Aspiration: food, drink or saliva entering the airway below the vocal folds.
こぼす（こぼす） — To spill food or liquid outside a container.
下げる（さげる） — In “clear the dishes,” this means removing used tableware.
冷ます（さます） — To cool something hot.
食品（しょくひん） — Food products used for eating or drinking.
食欲（しょくよく） — Appetite: the desire to eat.
水分補給（すいぶんほきゅう） — Replacing the fluids the body needs. Follow the person’s plan for how and how much to drink.
咳込む（せきこむ） — To cough repeatedly.
とろみ（とろみ） — Thickness or viscosity of a liquid. The term is not permission for a care worker to change it freely.
粉（こな） — Powder: fine particles. As a standalone word it is generally read kona. In the course expression とろみ（粉）, the reading ko is supplied for 粉, referring to powder used to adjust thickness.
つける（つける） — In “add thickness,” this means making a liquid more viscous.
飲み込む（のみこむ） — To swallow: moving material from the mouth through the throat into the esophagus.
一口大（ひとくちだい） — Bite-sized: small enough to fit in the mouth in one bite. It does not define the same suitable amount for everyone.
むせる（むせる） — A coughing response during eating or similar situations. This alone does not establish whether aspiration occurred.
量（りょう） — Amount: how much there is. Specify whether it is eaten or left over.
リーダー（りーだー） — Team leader: the person coordinating the team’s work.
記録（きろく） — Recording observations, statements and completed actions separately.
あげもの（あげもの） — Deep-fried dishes.
いためもの（いためもの） — Stir-fried dishes: ingredients heated while moved in a small amount of oil.
おやつ（おやつ） — A snack between main meals, or snack time.
粥（かゆ） — Rice porridge or a similar grain cooked in plenty of water. Its name alone does not establish suitability for swallowing.
お粥（おかゆ） — Polite form of 粥, meaning rice porridge.
カレーライス（かれーらいす） — Curry rice: rice served with curry beside or over it.
献立（こんだて） — Menu: the combination of dishes provided for a meal.
献立表（こんだてひょう） — A chart listing dishes for each meal.
主食（しゅしょく） — Staple food: a grain-based main component such as rice or bread.
汁物（しるもの） — Soup or another dish containing broth, such as miso soup.
ゼリー（ぜりー） — Gel dessert: a food made by setting a liquid. The name alone does not establish swallowing suitability.
たまご焼き（たまごやき） — A dish made by beating and cooking eggs.
漬物（つけもの） — Pickles: vegetables or other ingredients preserved in salt or seasoned liquid.
天ぷら（てんぷら） — Tempura: ingredients coated in batter and deep-fried.
豆腐（とうふ） — Tofu: a soybean food made by setting soy milk.
丼（どんぶり） — A large, deep bowl, or a dish of rice topped with ingredients in such a bowl. Use context to distinguish the meanings.
煮付け（につけ） — Simmering ingredients in seasoned liquid to absorb flavor, or a dish prepared this way.
煮物（にもの） — A dish simmered with liquid and seasonings.
ハンバーグ（はんばーぐ） — Hamburger steak: ground meat and other ingredients shaped and cooked.
副食（ふくしょく） — Side dishes eaten with the staple.
プリン（ぷりん） — A set dessert such as custard made with eggs and milk. Check ingredients for each product.
麦茶（むぎちゃ） — Barley tea: a drink made from barley.
メニュー（めにゅー） — A list of dishes offered; may refer to the meal plan.
焼き魚（やきざかな） — Grilled fish.
ヨーグルト（よーぐると） — Yogurt: a food made by fermenting milk or similar ingredients.

kaigo-language-session-3-notes.heading: Toileting terms, consent and sharing scope
paragraphs: “Urine” and “urge to urinate,” like “stool” and “urge for a bowel movement,” distinguish excreted material from sensation. A urinal receives urine, a toilet seat supports sitting, and a portable commode is movable toileting equipment. Names alone do not determine personal suitability or setup.

Raising or lowering pants means moving clothing up or down. Without an object, clarify rather than confuse this with clearing tableware. Modesty means embarrassment, but people do not all feel the same in every situation. Adapt conversation location and exposure to the person.

看護師 is read kangoshi, meaning nurse; 職員 is shokuin, meaning staff member. Not every facility worker is a nurse, so check roles when contacting someone. Recognize “enema” as a procedure term, but vocabulary knowledge is not training or authority to perform it.

[Explain in your own words] Are “the person reported an urge” and “urination was confirmed” identical? The first conveys a personal sensation; the second confirms actual urine passage. Do not infer one from the other. Record what was heard separately from what was confirmed.

kaigo-reading-new-220.heading: Learning conversation: distinguish location refusal from consultation refusal
paragraphs:
Person: I want to discuss toileting, but not here.
Worker: Other people are nearby. May we talk somewhere else?
Person: Yes. I have not told my family yet.
Worker: After hearing your concern, I will explain any necessary sharing.
Person: Please do not tell everyone first.
Worker: Understood. I will check a place first.

Reading: The person has not refused consultation itself, only talking in the current occupied location. Family has not been told. The worker will check a place first and explain necessary sharing after listening. Do not infer prior disclosure or a promise never to share under any circumstances.

kaigo-reading-new-221.heading: Learning conversation: check the final explanation scope
paragraphs:
Person: Please explain the call button tomorrow.
Worker: Understood. You want to rest now.
Person: But I want to know now just who is notified when I press it.
Worker: May I briefly explain only that?
Person: Yes. Please leave the rest until tomorrow.
Worker: Only the notification recipient for now.

Reading: The initial wish was to postpone explanation until tomorrow. The later request is to know the notification recipient now. Only that brief explanation is permitted now; the rest remains tomorrow. Preserve the final agreed scope, not just an intermediate statement.

kaigo-reading-new-222.heading: Learning conversation: writing difficulty versus communication
paragraphs:
Person: I want to write the time in the toileting record.
Worker: Could you write it here?
Person: I cannot use a pen, but I remember the time.
Worker: Could you tell me aloud? I will write it and read it back.
Person: That method, please.
Worker: I will ask the time now.

Reading: The person cannot write with a pen but remembers the time and wants to participate. They agreed to oral information, staff writing and reading back for confirmation. Asking the time is still ahead; record verification is not complete. Do not invent writing causes or memory problems.

kaigo-reading-new-223.heading: Learning conversation: distinguish this device’s buttons
paragraphs:
Worker A: This manual describes a confirm button and a call button.
Worker B: Does pressing confirm bring staff?
Worker A: No. Confirm only closes the display. Call notifies staff.
Worker B: This explanation is for this device?
Worker A: Yes. Check other devices in their own manuals.
Worker B: I will not assume function from names alone.

Reading: In this learning device, confirm closes the display and call notifies staff. Notification is not proof staff have arrived. Check each other device’s manual rather than assuming identical function from a button name.

kaigo-language-session-3-terms.heading: Vocabulary reference when needed
paragraphs: 上げる（あげる） — Raise: here, returning lowered clothing upward, as in pulling up pants.
足元（あしもと） — Feet and the area around them: check that clothing or equipment is not obstructing movement around the feet.
陰部（いんぶ） — Genital area: the external genitals and surrounding area. Respect privacy, check the necessary extent of care and minimize exposure.
おむつ（おむつ） — Diaper: an item worn to collect urine or stool. Its use does not establish the person’s overall abilities.
浣腸（かんちょう） — Enema: a procedure introducing liquid or another substance through the anus to encourage a bowel movement. Learning this word does not authorize you to perform it yourself.
着替える（きがえる） — Change clothes: take off the clothing being worn and put on other clothing.
下げる（さげる） — Lower: here, moving clothing downward, as in lowering pants.
失禁（しっきん） — Incontinence: urine or stool escaping involuntarily. It is not a reason to blame the person.
羞恥心（しゅうちしん） — Embarrassment: feeling embarrassed about being seen or having something known. Ask the person how they feel.
使い捨て手袋（つかいすててぶくろ） — Disposable gloves: gloves intended for one use. Remove them appropriately after dirty tasks and perform hand hygiene.
尿（にょう） — Urine: liquid produced by the kidneys that passes through the ureters, bladder and urethra to leave the body.
尿器（にょうき） — Urinal: a device for collecting urine. Knowing about a device is different from being able to select and use it appropriately.
尿意（にょうい） — Urge to urinate: the feeling of wanting to pass urine.
排泄（はいせつ） — Excretion: removing substances the body no longer needs. It includes urine and stool and also relates to processes such as sweating.
便（べん） — Stool: material that passes through the large intestine and other parts after digestion and absorption and leaves through the anus.
便意（べんい） — Urge to have a bowel movement: the feeling of wanting to pass stool.
便座（べんざ） — Toilet seat: the sitting surface that supports the body when using a toilet.
ポータブルトイレ（ポータブルトイレ） — Portable toilet: a movable toilet used in places such as a person’s room. Use it in a way appropriate to their condition and plan.
看護師（かんごし） — Nurse: a professional providing nursing care and assisting medical treatment. Report confirmed facts and consult them about changes in condition.
職員（しょくいん） — Staff member: a person working in the facility or organization. Distinguish people’s responsibilities when contacting them.
パジャマ（ぱじゃま） — Pajamas: clothing worn for sleep and similar occasions.
呼び出しボタン（よびだしボタン） — Call button: a button signaling that a staff member is needed. Check that it works, is within reach and the person understands and can use it.

141.title: Respect listening posture and personal boundaries
objectives: Do not assign one fixed meaning to expressions, gaze or posture.
Ask distance and touch preferences and check understanding and consent separately.
141.context: Consider a person stepping back from an approaching worker. Practice checking present wishes for distance and speech instead of applying general cultural assumptions.
141.artCaption: Use words, expression and pointing together to check wishes. One gesture does not establish understanding or consent.

142.title: Leave records that support continuity of care
objectives: Separate condition, actual help and personal responses in records.
Identify sources and unknowns and check receiver understanding and roles.
142.context: “Everything is fine” alone does not explain help or checked responses. Confirm necessary facts rather than filling unknown values or assessments.
142.artCaption: Handover in a quiet place includes receiver notes and questions. Sending differs from shared understanding.

143.title: Describe body areas from the person’s viewpoint
objectives: Distinguish trunk, upper- and lower-limb areas and sides.
Check indicated locations and complaints and report separately from assumed causes.
143.context: Consider checking and reporting “My hand hurts” with the indicated back of the right hand. Location knowledge does not establish diagnosis or transfer method.
143.artCaption: Check the indicated site and ask sides, times and sensations specifically. Do not apply one pictured area to every case.

144.title: Respect pace and advance information when guiding reduced vision
objectives: Check preferred guiding methods and route conditions before movement.
Describe corners or steps beforehand and adapt to responses.
144.context: Review pulling around a corner before explaining. This checks safe-movement conditions and wishes, not permission to try unfamiliar guiding.
144.artCaption: Introduce yourself first, check desired guiding and share pace and route changes.

145.title: Read wishes, responsibilities and sequences from conversations
objectives: Distinguish suggestions from choices and assigned roles from completed tasks.
Distinguish conditional future plans from completed facts.
145.context: Four learning conversations cover seats, inspection signatures, reservation checks and posting order. Do not invent completed travel or secured seats.
145.artCaption: Check wishes, abilities, environment and plans together. Consultation is not a completed-movement record.

146.title: Read eating information and requests accurately
objectives: Separate assistance scope, established intake and unknown intake.
Preserve weekday and display conditions and remaining undecided points.
146.context: Learning conversations cover bag opening, intake, weekday choices and menus. Do not use vocabulary to independently diagnose or change texture.
146.artCaption: Record dish-specific information and confirmed amounts separately. An object’s presence does not establish intake or completed serving.

147.title: Distinguish toileting consultation, consent and device functions
objectives: Check consultation location and explanation scope allowed now.
Distinguish writing from memory and button names from functions.
147.context: Read consultation locations, explanation limits, assisted writing checks and fictional button roles. Do not infer another device’s functions or personal abilities.
147.artCaption: Consider location and others nearby when discussing toileting. Wanting consultation differs from wanting to speak here now.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-nonverbal-dialo.prompt: The person steps back as staff approach. A colleague says everyone locally likes close distance. Which response is appropriate?
options: Maintain a comfortable distance and ask where to stand for conversation.
Approach again to show warmth.
Decide never to speak again because they stepped back.
Explain local customs and make them get used to closeness.
rationales: This checks present responses and wishes rather than cultural generalizations.
This repeats the approach without checking the withdrawal.
Distance preferences do not establish refusal of conversation.
Cultural tendencies do not justify requiring acceptance of proximity.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-shared-care-rec.prompt: A handoff says only “Everything is fine,” with no assistance or response details. What review is needed?
options: Fill unknown numbers with typical values to reassure the next worker.
Substitute “no abnormalities” for detailed information.
Omit records and receiver checks because it was said aloud.
Confirm and add times, condition, actual help, responses and unknowns, and share next checks with the receiver.
rationales: Never invent unmeasured numbers to complete records.
Changing wording still omits what was done and checked.
Speaking aloud differs from retaining needed records and shared understanding.
This specifies actual information and checks supporting continuing care.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-movement-body-l.prompt: The handoff says “arm pain,” but the person points to the back of their right hand. Which check is appropriate?
options: Use the facing worker’s right as the person’s right.
Confirm the back of the person’s right hand and report complaint time, words and observations separately from assumptions.
Diagnose the cause from pointing and hand over a disease name.
Omit the indicated location because an arm includes the hand.
rationales: Check sides from the person’s viewpoint without reversing them.
This identifies precise personal-side location and separates sources.
Location alone cannot diagnose a pain cause.
A broad area loses the indicated specific location.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-visual-guided-w.prompt: A worker pulls someone with reduced vision around a corner and explains afterward. What should change?
options: Check preferred guiding and pace, and explain direction before turning.
Detailed explanation afterward makes advance notice unnecessary.
Knowing the route removes the need to ask wishes.
Omit corners and steps and maintain one speed.
rationales: This aligns advance information, preferences and pace before movement.
Explanation afterward cannot replace information for preparation.
Route knowledge differs from checking suitable guidance.
Route changes and responses require pace checks too.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-209.prompt: Which matches the person’s wishes and the worker’s next action?
options: A window seat is wanted and already prepared.
Not going into the garden means no afternoon gathering.
The person will attend, prefers an entrance seat, and the worker will check the room.
Any seat is acceptable, so no check is needed.
rationales: Window seating was a suggestion, not the final choice; securing a seat is unconfirmed.
This confuses avoiding the garden with canceling participation.
This separates participation, seat preference and a future check.
An entrance preference exists and checking is planned.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-209.reading:
Person: I will attend the afternoon gathering, but I will not go into the garden.
Worker: Shall I arrange a seat by the window?
Person: It is too bright there. I would prefer a seat near the entrance.
Worker: Near the entrance. I will check the room now.
Person: Please do. I have not canceled my participation.
Worker: Right. Only your seating preference has changed.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-210.prompt: Which matches the inspection sheet’s entry, checking and signature?
options: Worker B entered and checked; the senior colleague already signed.
Worker B entered the number; a senior checked results. The signature request is still to come.
The senior entered the number; B checked and signed.
The senior’s check removes the need to request a signature.
rationales: This changes the checking actor and treats an outstanding signature as complete.
This accurately preserves roles and unfinished parts for three actions.
Entry and checking roles are reversed and signing is not established.
Completed checking can coexist with a planned signature request.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-210.reading:
Worker A: Is the wheelchair inspection sheet ready?
Worker B: I wrote the number. A senior colleague checked the results for me.
Worker A: So everything is finished?
Worker B: No, the signature is still missing.
Worker A: Who will sign?
Worker B: I will ask the senior colleague who checked it.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-211.prompt: Which matches the current reservation-change stage?
options: Reception confirmed and the person departed at the new time.
The wish confirms the change without reception.
Sharing a plan with colleagues means the person has received results.
The worker will ask reception, then inform the person after finding out. The person waits.
rationales: This invents completed confirmation and departure.
A wish alone does not establish availability; reception checking is planned.
Colleague plan sharing differs from giving the person results.
Availability checking and notification remain ahead, distinct from a completed change.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-211.reading:
Person: I would like to go to the library earlier.
Worker: First I will ask reception whether the reservation can be changed.
Person: Are we leaving right now?
Worker: No. I will let you know after confirming that a change is possible.
Person: All right. I will wait for a reply.
Worker: I will also tell another worker about the plan.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-212.prompt: What is the final confirmed order for the notice?
options: Check date, post, then show the person responsible.
Show the person responsible, post, then check date.
Check date, show the person responsible, then post.
Post first and check date and responsibility later.
rationales: This was the mistaken intermediate order, later corrected.
This moves the first date check to the end.
This includes the final correction and places presentation before posting.
Posting is last, not before checking.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-212.reading:
Worker A: Please prepare the notice. First check the date, next show it to the person responsible, and afterward post it.
Worker B: Post it and then show the person responsible?
Worker A: Those two are reversed.
Worker B: Check the date, have the person responsible check, then post it?
Worker A: Yes, that order for this notice, please.
Worker B: I will post it last.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-215.prompt: What assistance did the person request?
options: Read the small name label; the person opens the bag.
Open and empty the bag before reading.
Take over all eating because text is hard to see.
The person reads and opens without help.
rationales: This retains reading help and independent opening.
Opening help was not requested.
Text visibility does not establish eating ability or support needs.
Opening is independent, but reading was requested from staff.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-215.reading:
Person: I want to open the snack bag myself.
Worker: I will put it here, then.
Person: The name label is too small to read. Please read just that part.
Worker: I will read the label and hand you the unopened bag.
Person: Yes. I want to know what the snack is before eating.
Worker: Understood.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-216.prompt: Which intake and recording description is correct?
options: All staple, side dishes and soup are confirmed eaten.
Half staple, all side dishes and no soup.
Soup is unknown but correction is already finished.
All staple, half side dishes, soup unconfirmed; correction follows checking.
rationales: Side dishes were half and soup remains unconfirmed.
The amounts are reversed and no soup intake is not established.
B plans correction after soup checking, not completed correction.
This separates dish amounts from the future correction.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-216.reading:
Worker A: I am checking lunch records. Were both staple and side dishes half eaten?
Worker B: All the staple and half the side dishes.
Worker A: What about soup?
Worker B: I have not checked yet.
Worker A: Then please do not write that everything was eaten.
Worker B: I will check the soup amount before correcting the record.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-217.prompt: Which matches preference checks at the learning facility?
options: Snack time is three daily and seating is asked only Wednesday.
Wednesday snack is three, the seat is decided that day, and seating preferences are asked daily.
Wednesday snack and seat are both fully decided.
Selecting Wednesday seats means snack time cannot be chosen.
rationales: This changes both the selectable day and seating frequency.
This distinguishes weekday-limited time choice from daily seat checks.
Time is chosen but the seat remains undecided.
Wednesday snack time is selectable and three was requested.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-217.reading:
Person: Can I choose snack time next week too?
Worker: You can choose the time only on Wednesday.
Person: Can I choose a dining-room seat only that day too?
Worker: We ask seating preferences every day.
Person: Then Wednesday’s snack at three, please. I want to decide the seat that day.
Worker: Three for the time; the seat is still undecided.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-218.prompt: Which meets the requested menu conditions?
options: A large-print paper menu; the worker will check availability.
Large text on a screen.
Small text printed on paper.
Any format, recorded as already delivered.
rationales: This preserves both conditions and the future check.
Large text alone does not satisfy paper preference.
Paper alone does not satisfy large-print preference.
Both conditions matter and availability is still to be checked.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-218.reading:
Person: I would like a menu. Is there a printed paper version in large text?
Worker: A tablet can enlarge the text.
Person: I would prefer paper, rather than a screen.
Worker: Small text on paper would be hard to read?
Person: Yes, I need both conditions.
Worker: I will check for a large-print paper version.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-220.prompt: Which matches toileting-consultation wishes and staff plans?
options: Consultation itself was refused, so no location check.
Family already knows, so staff will not listen.
Check another location first; after listening, explain necessary sharing.
Promise no sharing under any circumstances instead of moving.
rationales: The refusal concerns an occupied location, not consultation itself.
The person has not told family and consultation is planned.
This respects location and preserves future listening and sharing explanation.
Necessary sharing will be explained later; no unconditional secrecy promise is made.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-220.reading:
Person: I want to discuss toileting, but not here.
Worker: Other people are nearby. May we talk somewhere else?
Person: Yes. I have not told my family yet.
Worker: After hearing your concern, I will explain any necessary sharing.
Person: Please do not tell everyone first.
Worker: Understood. I will check a place first.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-221.prompt: What explanation is finally permitted now?
options: Nothing now because tomorrow was requested first.
Briefly explain only who is notified; other details wait until tomorrow.
Explain every function because one detail is wanted now.
Notification waits until tomorrow; explain other functions now.
rationales: This ignores the later wish for notification details now.
This reflects the added wish and limits current scope.
Consent to one part is expanded to every function.
This reverses current and deferred topics.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-221.reading:
Person: Please explain the call button tomorrow.
Worker: Understood. You want to rest now.
Person: But I want to know now just who is notified when I press it.
Worker: May I briefly explain only that?
Person: Yes. Please leave the rest until tomorrow.
Worker: Only the notification recipient for now.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-222.prompt: Which matches the agreed recording method and present stage?
options: Staff guess the time because inability to write means inability to remember.
Write without reading back and mark checked.
Participation was refused, so no oral time question.
The person gives the time orally; staff write and read back. Asking the time is still ahead.
rationales: Do not infer memory difficulty from writing difficulty; ask the remembered time.
This omits agreed read-back and falsely completes it.
The person wants participation and agreed to oral communication.
This preserves remembered information and planned verification.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-222.reading:
Person: I want to write the time in the toileting record.
Worker: Could you write it here?
Person: I cannot use a pen, but I remember the time.
Worker: Could you tell me aloud? I will write it and read it back.
Person: That method, please.
Worker: I will ask the time now.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-223.prompt: Which describes this device’s buttons correctly?
options: Both confirm staff arrival.
Confirm notifies staff; call closes the display.
Confirm closes the display; call notifies staff. Notification alone does not prove arrival.
Identical names guarantee identical functions on other devices.
rationales: Neither closing nor notification is described as arrival confirmation.
The two functions are reversed.
This preserves both roles and notification versus arrival.
This learning device’s functions cannot be generalized.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-223.reading:
Worker A: This manual describes a confirm button and a call button.
Worker B: Does pressing confirm bring staff?
Worker A: No. Confirm only closes the display. Call notifies staff.
Worker B: This explanation is for this device?
Worker A: Yes. Check other devices in their own manuals.
Worker B: I will not assume function from names alone.
